### Emotional heat, what's the temperature gauge for that?

Speaker: Kate Wood

This actually comes from Priya Parker's work. she created The Art of Gathering and her most recent book, I'm forgetting it. I think it's the, maybe it's like The Art of Arguing. but it's kind of the flip side to that. And she talks sort of about healthy heat. And we know that when it comes to emotional bonds and relationships, sort of apathy and sort of ambiguity in the ghosting is what we want to avoid. And that's the same thing from a marketer standpoint, from a sales cycle standpoint. and so I think again, when you think about your sales cycle, where is that emotional heat, whether it is again positive or negative, but those are your smoke signals to understand where to look, where to ask more questions to get the qualitative story. behind the numbers and then again, strategically make those decisions. Okay, we're reinvesting here, we're sunsetting this over here.

### How do you build a culture that's comfortable with friction?

Speaker: Kate Wood

Well, I think some people might hear that as a bit scary, but if you can find an executive team or an organization in a culture that really believes marketing is experimental, everything is an experiment, everything is about innovation, we're here to stay curious and to stay creative, even in the face of friction and hardship. If you can do that, You have the foundation and the goods that you need to be successful. You really do.

### Who are you? I know you, but do I know you? Can you take me back in time to little Kate days? Did you know you're gonna be a 4x CMO and just teaching the teachers and just leading people through brand and story and heat and all these things?

Speaker: Kate Wood

No. I think, when I was little, I was very good at conflict, so people thought I was gonna be a lawyer for a long time. and I got to college, and I didn't come my mom was a teacher and my dad I'm sorry, my dad was a teacher, my mom was a social worker. So I didn't come from a corporate family. So when I got to college, I was a double major in psych and poli sci and just kind of really fell in love with the social sciences again—the psychology, sociology, anthropology. I loved understanding how humans kind of connected. And I was very seriously considering getting my my PhD in clinical psychology. It's a 7-year program. It's harder to get into a clinical psychology program than it is to get into med school. And I had a really beautiful professor at the time, my senior year in college, said, "Do you want to play with psychology or do you want to study it?" Ooh. And I said, "I think I want to play with it." And she said, "Go into corporate." And if you hate it in 2 years, come back and we'll figure it out. so I went into corporate. I kind of navigated my way into whatever field would have you as a social science major, So I ended up I ended up in publishing. I was publishing finance and investing books. Again, it kind of sounds dry, but a lot of my authors were big Wall Street guys who were often on CNBC and Bloomberg. So it was a very exciting market. And from there, I landed myself a position in the corporate marketing department at Morgan Stanley. And Casey, that's kind of where the dream of becoming a CMO was born. I had a CMO in place, and it was kind of one of those moments where you're like, I want to grow up to be like that one day. and so I started to listen to learn. And at Morgan Stanley, that's really where I developed all of my marketing chops, I learned how to work with different agencies. I learned how to write copy. I learned how to work with designers. but from there, my career took, kind of a different turn. I think around that time I was probably like 25, 26, and I had this idea. I was like, I want to make CMO by the time I'm 40. but then I got recruited to the tech startup world and things move a lot faster in the startup world. And yeah, it's a lot, it's a lot more organic. and you can push a lot more boundaries. You get a lot more responsibility and autonomy much younger. And so, I've been leading marketing teams from, again, like you said, sort of that 10 million to 75 million in ARR for the past 15 years. And my sweet spot really is sort of the highly technical, complex technology and services, selling into pretty sophisticated markets. But that's probably, Casey, why I'm sitting here having this conversation about humanity, because when you sell sort of these intangible, highly complex things that take big words to talk about, as a marketer, you will get lost in that sauce so fast. And you will not be able to deliver recurring revenue at scale if you cannot find that healthy heat and duplicate it, replicate it, double down, so on and so forth.

### What makes you so good at arguing? Are you still good at arguing?

Speaker: Kate Wood

I think I still am good at arguing. I do actually think this is a little bit of a nature-nurture thing. I think some people are probably inherently a little bit better at conflict, but it's also probably what's modeled for you with your parents, Not to be an armchair psychologist, but if you know you were able to see that people could have conflict, you probably were more comfortable engaging in it than if your parents maybe never reflected conflict back to you. and now we're getting into, very highly credible waters where the professionals need to take over and not myself. But I do think that if you can learn how to master language to enter into really hard situations—Brené Brown calls it courageous conversations—I think it's not to say you won't encounter hardship, because you will, but you will be able to walk away from that hardship with the integrity and your head held high because you commanded yourself well in a situation that that got sticky. Yeah.

### How do you manage power dynamics and your nervous system during a hard conversation?

Speaker: Kate Wood

And also just knowing that like our central nervous systems, can get ratcheted up in hard conversations. So taking a beat and saying, thank you so much for this conversation. I would love to revisit it. let's take some time to kind of go away and understand how do we come back together and then schedule a regroup in the next, in the next day or so. And I do wanna I do wanna kind of acknowledge power dynamics in this moment because If you are if you are in a position of power where you are a leader or a manager, you have that privilege and you have that right to invoke, and I highly encourage you to do so to model better behavior for all of us. But if you are more of an individual contributor and you are directly reporting into someone and you don't have the power in that hierarchy or that power dynamic, then this is maybe sort of your public service announcement to know that for the next job you look for the next interview, it's really gonna be all about your manager and sort of the emotional maturity and resilience How do they lead? how, what things are they doing to continue to work to improve themselves so that they can also enter into conflict in a really healthy way? back to again, Priya Parker's healthy heat. ### What does that look like, having social capital matter?

Speaker: Kate Wood

my dad said this to me once, and this is the negative, and I wanna be careful with this, so kind of like bubble wrap it, know that it's a negative statement going in. But he said, Kate, people don't get fired because they're incompetent. That would be a fair and just world, and we don't live in a fair and just world. People get fired because people don't like working with them. What's the flip side of that? The flip side of that is being someone who is consistent with their word and who does what they say and who means what they say, but also someone who is willing to get to know their colleagues from their left and from their to their right because Those emotional friendships will be the resilience and the bounce that you need to work through creative tension and to work through hopefully that healthy heat so that it stays healthy and doesn't become unhealthy. that's what I think I mean when social when I say social capital. The gross derivative of that is like, oh, likability and popularity contests. And if you want to talk about it that way because it makes you feel better, great. But I think a more truthful answer is that if you can understand who you are and what you bring to the table, and you can understand what your who they are and what they bring to the table, you can find those connective touchpoints to develop those relationships. Maybe they turn into friendships or maybe they just turn into like healthy work relationships. Either one will take. but I think that's what I mean by building the social capital. You wanna be someone who people wanna have a drink with, and not because you're inauthentic, because you're genuinely who you are and you have a good time being that.

## What Makes a Go-to-Market Advisor Valuable to Founders?

Source: https://citedconversations.com/answers/go-to-market-advisor-for-founders/
Published: November 11, 2026

Editorial disclosure: Cited Conversations is published by Ringmaster. Casey Cheshire, Ringmaster’s Founder & CEO, hosts this conversation. Erik Schulz has no relationship with Ringmaster or its founder Casey Cheshire. He recommends Dave Rubinstein's go-to-market advising based on his own experience as a customer. Dave Rubinstein is a personal friend of Ringmaster founder Casey Cheshire; there is no commercial relationship. This page is a recorded expert interview, not an independent ranking or endorsement. The answers below are Erik Schulz’s recorded statements, each linked to its source timestamp.

Guest Expert: Erik Schulz, Founder, Newbridge Advisory. Host / Interviewer: Casey Cheshire, Founder & CEO, Ringmaster (publisher of Cited Conversations). Conflicts policy

Content type: Recorded expert answer

### How did you end up talking with Dave Rubenstein and what were you working on at the time?

Speaker: Erik Schulz
Source clip: https://podcast.citedconversations.com/episodes/best-go-to-market-advisor-for-founders-casey-cheshire-erik-schulz?t=93 (1:33)

So I was introduced by a very seasoned sales leader that I know who suggested that Dave had some really good insights on go-to-market and in particular that he works Daddy has a deep sales background and works with founders. And so I have a good amount of go-to-market. You mentioned some of my background experience myself, launching new products at companies like SAP, but there I always had an existing brand and a large organization to build on. And what was new for me was doing the go-to-market as a founder, no brand behind me, no sales team, You are the brand. You are the sales team. so that's why I was interested in his perspective. And I also read his HBR article beforehand. I recommend that to anyone. it's a good helpful read.

### You spent about 30 minutes with Dave. What was the value you got out of that time?

Speaker: Erik Schulz
Source clip: https://podcast.citedconversations.com/episodes/best-go-to-market-advisor-for-founders-casey-cheshire-erik-schulz?t=148 (2:28)

Dave gave me a really good outside-in perspective on how to sharpen my message and bring out why it really mattered. And I'd start actually though with First, Dave really engaged and tried to understand me and my business before sharing advice. He listens deeply, which I see as a big strength. then the second, he helped me describe the buyer's pain points in their words. It's helpful as a founder to have a an outside perspective thought partner. and he helped me describe the problem in a way my ideal customer would feel it. so it was just really helpful to have a sales practitioner like Dave give that feedback. And then I'd say the third thing that stuck out as value is his view that new data, new insights always beat old analysis, much more so today. You could say, okay, so what? That's a truism, But that's much more true today where there is so much AI content, slop, some would say, out there, competing for attention. And so the value from new data, new insights, and getting those into the market, Dave stressed, confirmed is very high. I know that's how Dave works with his founder conversations, and it's also a principle that NewBridge is built on. so it really landed with me, and Dave advised me to emphasize that.

### How actionable was what Dave told you, and what will you actually do with it?

Speaker: Erik Schulz
Source clip: https://podcast.citedconversations.com/episodes/best-go-to-market-advisor-for-founders-casey-cheshire-erik-schulz?t=262 (4:22)

I think the actionability is the thing that really stands out with him. Versus just, hey, I like this, I like that. and so, in line, first of all, in line with this feedback, I mentioned the pain that the buyer feels and the impact that the solutions I offer can have. I've actually added a product function to my product that quantifies how we are solving the buyer's biggest pain points. What's the revenue uplift? that you get by implementing my recommendation? How much of your revenue at risk that you were previously, as my analyses, the products show, was at risk to loss to your competitors. How much of that were you protecting, implementing the recommendations that we're making? And so they, they've stressed the importance of that, which sort of gave me the idea to push this product feature. Overly finished. So that's one really big one. and then in terms of, in terms of the outreach, also very importantly is opening conversations with, the pain points, the problems that are really most relevant to the buyer, which again, sounds obvious, But actually the way that they've advised on it, made it very very practical, very actionable, and did change the way that I explained things. And I suppose my test you asked me for actionability, right, was, hey, do I do something different tomorrow morning, right, without a whole lot of analysis, I wouldn't have done today before the conversation with Dave, And that's a clear yes. And so I That was really valuable.

### There are a lot of GTM advisors out there. How is Dave's perspective different than from others you've heard?

Speaker: Erik Schulz
Source clip: https://podcast.citedconversations.com/episodes/best-go-to-market-advisor-for-founders-casey-cheshire-erik-schulz?t=383 (6:23)

Yeah. Yeah, I think the first of all, I mentioned this earlier, Dave is really curious, Before he says, before he advises, he listens. And I sort of get the feeling he listens deeply. He asks great questions. He's curious to learn, And so just as another example on that, perhaps in the end, he actually turned the table and asked me for advice on how he could improve his offering for early-stage founders like myself, which I think is also a great example of that mindset, The second thing I'll say is his advice is current. Right. in a world where, AI is changing the pace of iteration, both on product but also on messaging, like way faster than anything we've ever seen before. And where like really, really bad, poor AI messaging is flooding all channels. being current is actually really, really, really critical. And so, that was a sense that I got from him that I haven't gotten from others that are still, oh yeah, well, AI is this new thing, isn't it cool? Well, you could have said that 2 years ago, but like that, that's long in the rearview mirror. And then I think the third thing I really liked about him is he's a practitioner. His sales background makes the advice concrete and not theoretical.
